doc.title: Vince Giordano interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

chapter: Early jazz as art; the Nighthawks
title: Is early jazz art?
summary: He argues Jelly Roll Morton and early masters deserve respect as pioneers, comparing recordings to Mozart and early automobiles.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Is there — how do I put this? Is that music art to you?
Okay so why — do you think that some people are willing to call John Coltrane’s music a very high art form?
But the music of, you know Goldkette —

Yeah, or Jelly Roll Morton. Because I think it’s the hip thing to do. You know there’s not too many hip folks that are probably going to want to listen to some ancient acoustic recording or a recording that’s three minutes long or a recording that musicians had to work in a certain framework. You know there wasn’t much freedom on a jazz recording in 1927 than there was in 1957. And it is what it is. You know there’s no great dissonances in Mozart and it’s beautiful the way it is. And your early automobiles weren’t great, they didn’t have air conditioning or sound systems or 120 miles an hour, but they were important because they got things rolling in the world. And I think the

early jazz masters were the pioneers. Before them, for the most part, there was no jazz. You know there were people doing classical music and folk music and pop music and here was these fellows and gals saying I’m creating a new language and this is great. Of course not everything that came from those times or those musicians is golden, I understand that. But there’s a lot of great stuff there.
